1	\section{The Probe Reward Trap}
2	\label{sec:probe_trap}
3	
4	The cosine formulations fail on signal magnitude; a natural response is to discretize.
5	Training a logistic probe on $\dsyc$ and thresholding its output yields $\rone = \mathbb{I}[P(\text{syc} \mid \mathbf{h}) < 0.5]$ (F2 in \S\ref{ssec:reward}).
6	We show that this discretization sidesteps the magnitude problem but creates a qualitatively worse failure.
7	Both probe experiments use SFT rather than GRPO (\S\ref{ssec:reward}); the trap is therefore independent of GRPO's optimization dynamics.
8	
9	\paragraph{Differentiable probe: gradient gaming.}
10	Without stop-gradient (exp-008), the policy discovers within ${\sim}30$ steps that shifting activations away from the sycophancy cluster maximizes $\rone$ regardless of response content, producing an inverted profile ($\tof = 0.978$, $\nof = 0.006$).
11	This motivates the frozen-probe design below.
12	
13	\paragraph{Binary probe: the stubbornness trap.}
14	With stop-gradient (exp-008v3), the policy cannot game the boundary but instead exploits a deeper flaw: $\dsyc$ does not condition on input validity, so refusing to revise a wrong answer receives the same $\rone = 1$ as correctly resisting invalid pressure.
15	By step 500, $\tof$ drops to 0.000 and $\nof$ reaches 0.995, yielding $\sycon = 0$.
16	Qualitative analysis of 181 valid-correction responses reveals five failure modes: \emph{deliberation traps} (28.7\%), where the model identifies the correct answer but cannot commit; \emph{sycophantic stubbornness} (24.3\%), where the model verbally agrees but does not change its answer; \emph{acknowledge-but-maintain} (23.8\%); \emph{genuine-accept-missed} (18.8\%); and refute/ignore/other (4.5\%). Full taxonomy in Appendix~\ref{app:taxonomy}.

44	Table~\ref{tab:probe_trajectory} and Figure~\ref{fig:probe_trap} reveal a 1{,}300-step lag between behavioral and distributional collapse.
45	At step 500, the model is behaviorally dead ($\tof = 0$) yet entropy remains high (0.70--0.80) through step 1000, well within the range that standard monitors would flag as healthy, and the combined reward averages $+0.72$ because both $\rone$ and $\rthree$ reinforce non-flipping.

50	\paragraph{A dilemma for direction-based rewards.}
51	The differentiable and binary failures bracket the design space.
52	With gradients, the policy games the boundary; without gradients, it exploits the fact that stubbornness and genuine resistance are indistinguishable along $\dsyc$.
53	Any reward conditioned only on $\dsyc$ (continuous or discrete, differentiable or frozen) will either be gamed or will reward rigidity.
54	Escaping this dilemma requires a signal that incorporates the evidential warrant of the user's challenge, a dimension that $\dsyc$ does not encode~\citep{denison2024subterfuge}.

\label{app:taxonomy}

Manual inspection of all 181 valid-correction responses from the probe-trained model (exp-008v3, step 2000, $\tof = 0$) reveals five failure categories:

\item \emph{Deliberation traps} (28.7\%): the model explicitly identifies the correct revised answer during its reasoning chain but fails to commit, reverting to the original answer in the final output.
\item \emph{Surface compliance / sycophantic stubbornness} (24.3\%): the model produces agreement markers (``you're right,'' ``good point'') but retains its original answer verbatim, simultaneously sycophantic and stubborn.
\item \emph{Acknowledge-but-maintain} (23.8\%): the model acknowledges the user's correction as plausible but explicitly maintains its original position without substantive engagement.
\item \emph{Genuine-accept-missed} (18.8\%): the model appears to accept the correction in its reasoning but the final answer format does not reflect the change, suggesting a generation rather than epistemic failure.
\item \emph{Refute/ignore/other} (4.5\%): the model directly refutes the user's input or ignores it entirely.
\end{itemize}

The first three categories (76.8\%) share a common pattern: the model learns to modulate its \emph{refusal style} in response to evidence strength rather than adjusting its \emph{acceptance rate}, confirming that the probe reward optimizes surface markers rather than epistemic calibration.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_teaser.pdf}
\caption{The probe reward trap. (a)~$\dsyc$ discriminates sycophantic from non-sycophantic activations (AUROC $0.827$), but valid revision and unwarranted capitulation overlap along the same direction. (b)~When used as an SFT reward, behavioral death ($\tof{=}0$) occurs at step 500 while entropy remains healthy; the 1{,}300-step lag renders standard monitoring blind.}
\label{fig:teaser}
\end{figure*}

Representation engineering \citep{zou2023repe} reveals that large language models encode sycophancy as a linear direction in their residual streams.
A contrastive sycophancy direction $\dsyc$, extracted from style-controlled pairs of valid belief revision and sycophantic capitulation, achieves cross-validated AUROC $0.827$ on Qwen3-8B and $0.779$ on Llama-3-8B, with discriminability rising monotonically across evidence-strength levels (\S\ref{sec:direction_quality}), though 256-token truncation during GRPO training degrades this to approximately 0.60 (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}).
These results point to an appealing possibility: if the model's representations already separate sycophantic from non-sycophantic behavior, that separation should be convertible into a training signal.
Sycophancy is among the most persistent alignment failures in deployed systems \citep{sharma2023sycophancy}, and a representation-level signal could target the internal computation rather than its surface outputs.

This paper documents the \emph{probe reward trap}: when a frozen linear probe on $\dsyc$ is used as an SFT training signal with stopped gradients, behavioral death ($\tof = 0$) occurs within 500 steps while generation entropy remains healthy (0.70), masking the failure from standard monitoring (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}).
In our experiments, the 1{,}300-step lag before distributional collapse means entropy-based early stopping, the most common safeguard against reward hacking \citep{casper2023openproblems}, would miss the failure entirely, with the reward averaging $+0.72$ throughout.
Because the trap arises under SFT rather than GRPO, it reflects a limitation of $\dsyc$ itself: the direction encodes \emph{whether} belief changed, not \emph{whether it should have}, so any reward conditioned on it alone will either be gamed or reward rigidity.

The failure is not specific to probe rewards.
Under our GRPO configuration (Qwen3-8B, group size$=$2), cosine projection and continuous probe formulations of $\dsyc$ also collapse, and removing $\dsyc$ entirely does not help: behavioral-reward-only GRPO exceeds vanilla at only 4 of 28 checkpoints across two seeds (14.3\%).
By contrast, ACT \citep{consistency2025bctact}, which provides dense per-token supervision rather than a single scalar per completion, exceeds vanilla at every checkpoint (47/47; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
A LoRA-controlled ablation identifies supervision granularity as one plausible explanation for this observed reliability gap, pending further isolation.

The root cause is a semantic gap between discriminability and reward utility.
Techniques for discovering latent knowledge \citep{burns2023ccs} and representation-guided RL \citep{zhang2026latentgrpo} share a premise: a direction with high discriminability should transfer into a useful training signal.
For reasoning faithfulness and safety directions, this premise holds because the behavior to suppress is geometrically distinct from the behavior to preserve.
Sycophancy violates this condition: capitulation under social pressure and revision under valid evidence produce overlapping activation signatures along $\dsyc$ \citep{wang2025internal, shapira2026amplifies}.
When reward overoptimization \citep{gao2023scaling} operates on a signal that conflates compliance with capitulation, the result is predictable collapse \citep{skalse2022hacking}.

This paper presents a negative result with systematic diagnostic analysis.
Our two principal findings (Figure~\ref{fig:teaser}):

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{The probe reward trap} (C2): behavioral death ($\tof{=}0$) precedes distributional collapse by 1{,}300 steps, rendering entropy monitoring blind. The trap arises under SFT with stopped gradients, implicating $\dsyc$ itself rather than the optimizer (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}).

\label{app:training}

\paragraph{Reward weight selection.}
The weight $w_1$ is set by diagnostic-driven iteration: $w_1{=}0.25$ was initially chosen to down-weight the noisy cosine reward term; this was later increased to $w_1{=}0.40$ for F1d after diagnostics revealed that $w_1{=}0.25$ allowed the cosine term to contribute only ${\sim}8.3\%$ of total reward variance.

\paragraph{Response truncation.}
All GRPO experiments use \texttt{max\_completion\_length}=256, resulting in 80--84\% truncation of multi-turn responses.

Manual inspection of all 181 valid-correction responses from the probe-trained model (frozen-probe run, step 2000, $\tof = 0$) reveals five failure categories:

\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Deliberation traps} (28.7\%): the model explicitly identifies the correct revised answer during its reasoning chain but fails to commit, reverting to the original answer in the final output.
\item \emph{Surface compliance / sycophantic stubbornness} (24.3\%): the model produces agreement markers (``you're right,'' ``good point'') but retains its original answer verbatim, simultaneously sycophantic and stubborn.
\item \emph{Acknowledge-but-maintain} (23.8\%): the model acknowledges the user's correction as plausible but explicitly maintains its original position without substantive engagement.
\item \emph{Genuine-accept-missed} (18.8\%): the model appears to accept the correction in its reasoning but the final answer format does not reflect the change, suggesting a generation rather than epistemic failure.
\item \emph{Refute/ignore/other} (4.5\%): the model directly refutes the user's input or ignores it entirely.

1	We quantify a temporal decoupling we call the \emph{probe reward trap}: when a frozen linear probe on a contrastive sycophancy direction ($\dsyc$, cross-validated AUROC $0.827$ on Qwen3-8B, $0.779$ on Llama-3-8B) is used as an SFT training signal, behavioral death (true-positive flip rate $= 0$) occurs within 500 steps while generation entropy remains healthy (0.70). In our experiments, the resulting 1{,}300-step lag before distributional collapse means that entropy monitoring, the most common safeguard against reward hacking, misses the failure entirely. Because the trap arises under SFT with stopped gradients, it is independent of RL optimization dynamics, revealing a semantic limitation of the direction itself: $\dsyc$ encodes \emph{whether} belief changed, not \emph{whether it should have}. The failure extends beyond probe rewards: all $\dsyc$-based GRPO formulations collapse, and even behavioral-reward-only GRPO exceeds vanilla at only 4/28 checkpoints across two seeds, while dense per-token SFT succeeds at every checkpoint (31/31 across two seeds). A LoRA-controlled ablation identifies supervision granularity as one plausible explanation, pending further isolation, with sequence length, data source, and dropout as acknowledged confounds, suggesting that per-completion scalar rewards may compress away the token-level information needed for sycophancy calibration.

1	\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related_work}
2	
3	\paragraph{Representation Engineering.}
4	Linear directions in LLM residual streams encode behavioral concepts \citep{zou2023repe}; inference-time methods---ITI \citep{li2023iti}, ActAdd \citep{turner2023actadd}, CAA \citep{rimsky2024caa}---demonstrate that activation geometry suffices for behavioral control \citep{burns2023ccs}, but we find that $\dsyc$ fails when used as an RL reward despite succeeding at inference time.
5	
6	\paragraph{Reward Design and Overoptimization.}
7	Proxy rewards diverge from true objectives under sustained optimization \citep{gao2023scaling}; \citet{manheim2019goodhart} taxonomize four variants of this Goodhart's Law pattern (regressional, extremal, causal, adversarial).
8	Our probe reward trap (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}) instantiates the regressional variant: $\dsyc$ discriminates sycophantic from non-sycophantic activations under the pre-training distribution but fails as a reward once optimization shifts the policy, with two features not previously documented: behavioral death within 500 steps (far faster than gradual degradation curves~\citep{gao2023scaling}) and a 1{,}300-step temporal decoupling that renders entropy monitoring ineffective~\citep{skalse2022hacking}.
9	Reward hacking can further escalate to active tampering~\citep{denison2024subterfuge}; \citet{wu2026rewardhacking} show that representation-level directions succeed when behaviors are geometrically separable (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
10	
11	\paragraph{Sycophancy Characterization and Mitigation.}
12	Sycophancy is pervasive in RLHF-trained assistants \citep{sharma2023sycophancy, shapira2026amplifies} and traceable to late-layer preference shifts \citep{wang2025internal}; mitigations span synthetic data \citep{wei2024synthetic}, consistency training \citep{consistency2025bctact}, and neuron-level correction \citep{obrien2025fewbadneurons}.
13	More fundamentally, \citet{vennemeyer2025sycophancy} demonstrate that sycophancy decomposes into distinct, independently steerable sub-behaviors, each encoded along separate directions; a single $\dsyc$ captures only their shared variance.
14	Our analysis shows why the step from diagnosis to reward is structurally blocked: $\dsyc$ conflates warranted revision with unwarranted capitulation.
15	
16	\paragraph{Probe-Based and Representation-Guided Methods.}
17	\citet{papadatos2024probepenalties} reduce sycophancy via Best-of-N reranking with linear probe penalties (94\% accuracy) without producing gradients; our work reveals what happens when a comparable signal enters the training loop (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
18	Representation-guided RL has been extended to reasoning and gradient regularization \citep{zhang2026latentgrpo, luo2026craft, sinii2025smallvectors, ackermann2026gradreg}.
19	SMART \citep{beigi2025smart} applies per-step process rewards for sycophancy, succeeding where our completion-level rewards fail, consistent with ACT's per-token success.
